pottery.name: Pottery
pottery.title: Pottery classes: what to expect and how to start · Epic Events
pottery.description: Wheel or hand-building, what a first class is like, how many lessons before you can work alone, and how to do pottery at home.
pottery.intro: A pottery class is two or three hours with your hands in wet clay, learning to throw on the wheel or build by hand while a potter shows you how. Most beginners make two or three small pieces, which the studio fires and glazes for you to collect a few weeks later. It suits anyone who wants to make something real; no experience needed.

photos.alt: Three speckled white stoneware bottles, one holding dried poppy heads

photos.want: To license: hands building a coil pot on a table
To license: glazed bowls on a studio shelf

blocks.img: A wheel and a hand-building table side by side in a studio, mid-class
p: There are two ways to make a pot, and most studios teach both. Neither is the easy option: the wheel is quicker once it clicks, and hand-building gives you more control from the start.

compare.line: Clay spins on a wheel head and you shape it with wet hands. This is called throwing.
pts: Best for round things: bowls, mugs, cups, vases
The hard part is centring the clay; it takes a few goes
A first class usually gets you two or three small pieces
Messier: expect to get wet up to the elbows

compare.line: You shape clay on a table by pinching it, rolling coils or cutting slabs.
pts: Best for anything that isn't round: plates, planters, tiles, sculpture
Slower and calmer, and easier to fix as you go
Good for children and anyone with weaker hands
Needs no machine, so you can carry on at home

p2: If you can't choose, book a taster that does a bit of both. Most people know within an hour which one they want to go back to.

blocks.img: Centring: wet hands pressing a spinning mound of clay, close up
blocks.h2: What your first class is like
p: A first class is usually two to three hours, with six to ten people and one potter. You don't need to bring anything. This is how most wheel tasters run:

steps.d: Ten minutes watching the potter throw a pot from start to finish, so you know what you're aiming for.
You knead your clay like bread dough to push out air bubbles, which would crack the pot in the kiln.
The clay goes on the wheel and you press it into a smooth, even mound. It's the hardest step, and the potter will help.

steps.t: Opening and pulling up the walls
steps.d: You press a hole into the middle, then draw the clay upwards between your fingers to make the walls.
Most beginners make three or four attempts and keep one or two. Those stay at the studio to dry.

p2: Trimming and glazing come later. Some studios book you back for a glazing session; others glaze your pieces in a colour you pick on the day.

blocks.img: A potter in a clay-smeared apron, sleeves rolled up, grinning
p: Aprons, clay and tools are provided. Wear things you won't mind marking.

list.d: Clay washes out of cotton, but the wet clay (slip) splashes. Short or rolled-up sleeves.
Long nails dig into the clay on the wheel and leave marks. Trim them if you can.
Clay gets into them and they scratch the pot. Tie long hair back.
You work a foot pedal on the wheel, and studio floors can be wet.

note.d: Dry clay dust contains silica, which you shouldn't breathe. Good studios clean with water and sponges, never by sweeping.

blocks.img: Kiln door open on a shelf of pale bisque pots, next to the same pots glazed
blocks.h2: Firing, and when you get your pots back
p: Your pots aren't finished when you leave. They go through two firings in a kiln, which is why it takes weeks, not days.

head: Stage
What happens
How long
rows: The pot is turned upside down when leather-hard, and the base is shaped
A few days after your class
It dries slowly until bone-dry, or it cracks in the kiln
The first firing, to about 1,000°C, turns clay into ceramic
Dipped or brushed with glaze, by you or the studio
Earthenware to about 1,100°C, stoneware to about 1,250°C

p2: All in, expect three to six weeks. Studios wait for a full kiln before firing, so busy months can take longer.

blocks.img: A row of first attempts on a shelf, from wobbly to good
blocks.h2: How many classes before you can work on your own?
p: Most people make a simple pot in their first session, with help. Working alone takes longer, and the thing that holds people up is centring: pressing the clay into a steady, even mound on the wheel. Some get it in a few sessions and some take months. Both are normal.

steps.d: One session to find out whether you like it, and whether you prefer the wheel or your hands.
Centring, a cylinder, a bowl, then trimming and glazing what you made.

steps.t: A second term, or a few months of weekly practice
steps.d: The point where pots start coming out the way you meant them to.
After about 15 to 20 sessions, most people throw reliably and are ready for an open-studio membership or a set-up at home.

p2: Hand-building is quicker to take home: after one or two classes you can carry on by yourself, as long as you have somewhere to fire.

note.d: Going regularly matters more than going for long. Skills fade over long gaps.

blocks.img: A small electric kiln and a work table in a tidy garage
p: You can make pots at home with or without a kiln. What you need depends on whether you want to fire them.

list.d: Needs no firing. Good for models and practice, but it isn't waterproof or food-safe.
Many studios and paint-your-own cafés will fire pieces you made at home, for a fee.
Plugs into a normal 13-amp socket, holds roughly 16 to 60 litres and reaches stoneware temperatures, about 1,300°C.
Needs its own electricity supply, fitted by an electrician.
A kiln needs space, ventilation and distance from anything that burns. Garages and sheds are common.
Tabletop wheels exist, but a full-size wheel is easier to centre on. Many people throw at a studio and hand-build at home.
Never pour clay water down the drain: it sets and blocks pipes. Let it settle in a bucket and pour off the clear water.
Dried-out clay can be soaked, dried back to the right firmness and used again.

note.d: Dry clay dust contains silica. Clean with a damp sponge or mop, never sweep. Wear a fitted P2 mask for dusty jobs, and keep the workspace apart from where you live.

blocks.img: A busy open-studio evening: several potters at their wheels, chatting
p: Pottery is more sociable than it looks. Most people who stay with it do so for the people as much as the pots.

list.d: Most run with six to ten people, and the same faces each week.
After a course, many studios offer membership: wheel time, shelf space, firing, and a community of potters.
Many counties and towns have a potters' guild, with demonstrations, exhibitions and shared kilns. Search for your county's potters' guild.
The UK's association for potters, founded in 1958. It runs the Contemporary Ceramics Centre in Bloomsbury, London, publishes Ceramic Review, and anyone can join as an Associate member.
Ceramic Art London each spring, and the British Ceramics Biennial in Stoke-on-Trent.
The Great Pottery Throw Down has brought a wave of new beginners into studios.

blocks.img: Children's clay-covered hands holding a pinch pot (hands only, no faces)
p: Clay is one of the best things to do with children: it's forgiving, it's messy in a good way, and they take something home. What works depends on age.

head: Age
What works
The wheel?
rows: Pinch pots, handprints and squashing clay, with a grown-up alongside
Hand-building: coil pots, tiles, little animals
Usually, once their feet reach the pedal
Many studios take them in adult beginners' classes

note.d: Every children's event on Epic says who it's for. Drop-off sessions are run by a Checked host.

faqs: Do I need any experience?
No. Beginners' classes and tasters assume you've never touched clay. The potter shows you each step, and most people make something they're happy to keep on their first go.
Is the wheel or hand-building better for beginners?

Neither is easier, they're different. The wheel is faster once you can centre the clay, and it's the one most people want to try. Hand-building is calmer, needs no machine and is easier to carry on at home. A taster that does both is a good way to choose.
How long until I get my pots back?
Usually three to six weeks. Pots are trimmed, dried for a week or two, then fired twice. The studio tells you when they are ready to collect.
How many lessons until I can throw on my own?
Most people throw reliably after about 15 to 20 sessions: a beginners' course of 6 to 8 weeks, then a second term or a few months of weekly practice. Centring is the step that takes longest.
Can I do pottery at home without a kiln?
Yes. Air-dry clay needs no firing, though it isn't waterproof or food-safe. Or make pieces in real clay at home and pay a studio to fire them.
Is pottery safe for children?
Yes. Clay is non-toxic, and children's sessions use hand-building, with the wheel from about age 8. The one thing to avoid is dry clay dust, so good studios clean with water, never by sweeping.
What should I wear?
Old clothes with short or rolled-up sleeves, flat closed shoes, and no rings or watches. Short nails help on the wheel. Aprons and tools are provided.
Is clay dust dangerous?
Dry clay dust contains silica, which can damage your lungs if you breathe it over time. Clean with a damp sponge or mop, never sweep, and wear a fitted P2 mask for dusty jobs.

fossil-hunting.name: Fossil hunting
fossil-hunting.title: Fossil hunting in the UK: where, when and how · Epic Events
fossil-hunting.description: The best UK beaches for fossils, when to go, what you'll find, how to stay safe with the tides, and the rules for collecting.
fossil-hunting.intro: Fossil hunting is walking a beach where the cliffs are slowly crumbling, and looking for the remains of animals that lived millions of years ago. Most finds are loose on the beach, washed out by the sea. You need no experience, just the right beach, the right tide and a good eye.

photos.want: To license: an ammonite in an open hand, on shingle
To license: Charmouth beach and cliffs at low tide
To license: belemnites and crinoids on a pebble beach, close up

blocks.img: The Jurassic Coast at Charmouth: grey cliffs and a long beach at low tide
p: Fossils turn up where soft rock is wearing away into the sea. These are the best-known places in the UK.

list.t: The Jurassic Coast, Dorset and East Devon
list.d: A UNESCO World Heritage Site. Charmouth and Lyme Regis are the best-known beaches for ammonites and belemnites.
Staithes, Runswick Bay, Robin Hood's Bay, Boggle Hole and Saltburn, for Jurassic fossils.
Compton Bay and Hanover Point for dinosaur footprints at low tide, and bone fragments at Brook and Compton.
Herne Bay, for shark teeth.
Hunstanton, with its striped cliffs and marine fossils.
Birling Gap, under the Seven Sisters chalk cliffs.
White Park Bay, County Antrim, for belemnites, ammonites and gryphaea.

blocks.img: A winter beach after a storm, fresh cliff fall and a falling tide
p: Timing matters more than the beach. The same stretch can be bare one day and full of finds the next.

list.d: Storms and rough seas break down the cliffs and wash new fossils onto the beach.
Set out as the tide goes out, so you have the most beach and the most time.

list.t: Check the tide before you leave
list.d: Some beaches, such as Monmouth Beach at Lyme Regis, are only safe around low tide.

p: Most first finds are one of these.

tiles.want: A ribbed ammonite in a pebble

tiles.d: The bullet-shaped part of a squid-like animal.
tiles.where: Jurassic Coast, Yorkshire, White Park Bay

tiles.want: A gryphaea in an open hand

tiles.d: Star-shaped stem pieces of a "sea lily".
Prints set in the rock ledges; bone fragments too.
tiles.want: A three-toed print in a ledge at low tide

p2: To spot them, walk the high-tide line, where finds collect, and look for stones with an odd shape, a ridge or a pattern. Many fossils sit inside rounded pebbles.

blocks.img: A walker on the beach well back from the cliff base, tide going out
p: The sea and the cliffs are the two dangers, and both are easy to avoid if you plan.

list.d: Go on a falling tide. The sea comes in fast and can cut you off.
Keep well clear of the cliff base and of mudflows. Rockfalls and landslips happen without warning, especially after bad weather.
Say where you're going and when you'll be back. Phone signal is patchy on many beaches.
Wear safety glasses if you split stones with a hammer.

note.t: If someone is in trouble on the coast,
note.d: call 999 and ask for the Coastguard.

blocks.img: Fossils lying loose on the shingle below the cliffs
p: Collecting is allowed on most UK beaches, within a few rules.

steps.t: Collect loose material from the beach
steps.d: Not from the cliffs. Never dig or hammer into a cliff.
Some sites are Sites of Special Scientific Interest, where collecting is restricted. Check before you go.

steps.t: In West Dorset, follow the Fossil Collecting Code
steps.d: It applies between Lyme Regis and Burton Bradstock. Report important finds to the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre, and offer important specimens to a UK museum before selling them.

steps.t: In Scotland, follow the Scottish Fossil Code
steps.d: Scotland has its own code for collecting.

blocks.img: Boots, a hand lens, a tide table and finds wrapped in kitchen paper, laid out
p: Nothing specialist, unless you want to split stones.

list.d: Shingle and weedy rock ledges are hard going in trainers.
For that beach, checked before you set off.
For the tide, photos of finds, and emergencies.
To wrap finds so they don't knock together.

list.t: A geological hammer and safety glasses
list.d: Only if you want to split stones, and only on loose pebbles.

blocks.img: An adult and a child from behind, crouched over the shingle (no faces)
p: It's one of the best days out for children: free, outdoors, and every child can find something.
On the Jurassic Coast, the guided walks run by Lyme Regis Museum and the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre are the best way to start. The guides show you where to look and identify what you find.

note.d: Keep children away from the bottom of the cliffs, and hold hands near the water's edge.

blocks.img: A heritage centre volunteer identifying a find for a visitor
p: Once you've found a few, it's easy to go deeper.

list.d: At the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre and local museums.
Local geology groups, and the Geologists' Association, run field trips.
Lyme Regis Fossil Festival.

faqs: Where is the best place to find fossils in the UK?
The Jurassic Coast in Dorset and East Devon, especially Charmouth and Lyme Regis. The Yorkshire coast around Robin Hood's Bay and the Isle of Wight are close behind.
When is the best time to go fossil hunting?
In winter, after storms, on a falling tide. Storms bring down the cliffs and wash new fossils onto the beach, and a falling tide gives you the most beach for the longest time.
Can I keep what I find?
On most UK beaches, yes, if it was lying loose. Some sites are protected and restrict collecting. In West Dorset, the Fossil Collecting Code asks you to report important finds.
Do I need a hammer?
No. Most finds are loose on the beach. If you split pebbles, use a geological hammer and safety glasses, and never hammer the cliffs.
Is fossil hunting safe for children?
Yes, if you check the tide, stay away from the bottom of the cliffs and hold hands near the water. A guided walk is an easy first trip.
What does a fossil look like on a beach?
Look for stones with an odd shape, a ridge or a pattern: a spiral, a bullet shape, a star. Walk the high-tide line, where finds collect. Many fossils sit inside rounded pebbles.
What should I do if I find something big?
Leave it where it is, take photos and note exactly where it is. On the Jurassic Coast, tell the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre; elsewhere, a local museum.
